chunks.text: The chain rule differentiates composite functions, where one function is nested inside another, such as f(g(x)).
The chain rule states d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x): differentiate the outer function evaluated at the inner function, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
In Leibniz notation, if y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du)·(du/dx), where the du terms appear to cancel even though they are limits rather than literal fractions.
The most common chain-rule error is forgetting to multiply by the derivative of the inner function after differentiating the outer function.
To identify the inner and outer functions, ask which operation would be performed last when evaluating the expression at a number; that last operation is the outer function.
For (3x + 7)⁵, the outer function is the fifth power and the inner function is 3x + 7, so the derivative is 5(3x + 7)⁴·3 = 15(3x + 7)⁴.
For sin(4x²), the derivative is cos(4x²)·8x = 8x cos(4x²), where cos(4x²) is the outer derivative and 8x is the inner derivative.
For a power composition, d/dx[g(x)ⁿ] = n·g(x)ⁿ⁻¹·g'(x).
For a sine composition, d/dx[sin(g(x))] = cos(g(x))·g'(x); for cosine, d/dx[cos(g(x))] = −sin(g(x))·g'(x).
For an exponential composition, d/dx[e^(g(x))] = e^(g(x))·g'(x).
For a logarithm composition, d/dx[ln(g(x))] = g'(x)/g(x).
When the inner function is simply x, its derivative is 1, which is why the basic derivative rules look as though they involve no chain step.
For multi-layer compositions, apply the chain rule from the outside inward, generating one factor for each layer of nesting.
Differentiating ((2x + 1)³ + 5)⁴ gives 4((2x + 1)³ + 5)³·6(2x + 1)² = 24(2x + 1)²((2x + 1)³ + 5)³, because the three layers produce three multiplied factors.
When the chain rule combines with the product or quotient rule, identify the outermost structure first and apply that rule, then handle the inner derivatives one at a time.
For x²·(5x − 1)⁴, the product rule gives 2x(5x − 1)⁴ + x²·20(5x − 1)³, which factors to 2x(5x − 1)³(15x − 1).
For e^(sin x), the derivative is cos x·e^(sin x): the exponential is its own outer derivative and cos x is the inner derivative of sin x.
Naming intermediate variables in Leibniz notation (y depends on u, u depends on v, v depends on x) helps organize nested chain-rule computations and reduces errors.
A useful self-check for any composite-function derivative: if the answer contains no factor coming from the inner function, the chain rule was likely applied incorrectly.

The chain rule analogy of chained rates: if a rod expands 0.01 inches per degree and temperature rises 2 degrees per hour, the rod expands 0.01·2 = 0.02 inches per hour, mirroring how the chain rule multiplies the outer and inner rates.
The chain rule underlies implicit differentiation, related rates, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus with a variable limit, making it one of the most reused tools in the course.
